title: Nvidia Partners With Wall Street Giants to Raise $500 Billion for AI Infrastructure
excerpt: The chipmaker signed agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to create compute financing platforms for AI data center buildout.
body:
• Nvidia signed memorandums of understanding with six major financial firms to raise over $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure.
  • CEO Jensen Huang said Nvidia has the option to backstop up to $125 billion, or 25% of potential deals through the platforms.
  • The initiative creates "compute financing platforms" that offer capital at attractive rates to Nvidia customers building AI data centers.

Nvidia announced Monday it has partnered with six of Wall Street's largest financial institutions to launch compute financing platforms targeting over $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure. The chipmaker signed memorandums of understanding with Apollo Global Management, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs, and KKR, according to Reuters and the Financial Times, which first reported the deal.

CEO Jensen Huang said on X that Nvidia has the option to backstop up to $125 billion — 25% of potential deals struck through the platforms.

"These financing platforms will help customers access scarce compute at scale and build the AI factories that will power every industry and country in the age of AI."

— Jensen Huang, CEO, Nvidia

How the Financing Platforms Work

The agreements establish what Nvidia calls "compute financing platforms" — dedicated pools of capital designed to give the company's customers access to funds at "attractive rates" for building AI data centers and purchasing computing hardware. The platforms target frontier AI developers, enterprises, governments, and cloud providers who need large-scale access to Nvidia's chips and AI infrastructure.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=asb9L48ROXE

For the six financial partners, the arrangement creates longer-duration, usage-linked investment opportunities. Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said Nvidia's "full-stack platform is in high demand and uniquely positioned at the centre of that global buildout," adding that the bank is "excited for the new opportunity to create a market for credit backed by Nvidia compute," according to The Times.

Nvidia did not disclose financial terms, individual firm commitments, or a timetable for deploying the $500 billion. The agreements are memorandums of understanding, meaning final terms have yet to be hammered out.

Context: The AI Spending Arms Race

The deal underscores the staggering scale of capital flowing into AI infrastructure. Big Tech companies have signaled that AI spending will not slow down, with combined outlays set to surpass $730 billion this year, according to Reuters. Goldman Sachs estimates that total spending on chips, power generation, and data centers will reach $1.64 trillion by the end of the decade.

Nvidia's move follows a pattern of the chipmaker embedding itself deeper into the financial architecture of the AI boom. The company has made 66 private-company investments across 2025 and 2026, according to FactSet data cited by Barron's. Last month, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia was in talks to provide roughly $250 billion in financing guarantees for OpenAI's 10-gigawatt data center project in southern Ohio, developed by SoftBank's energy subsidiary.

The financing platform model is not entirely new to the sector. Apollo and Blackstone earlier this year struck a similar deal with Broadcom to set up a compute financing platform for that chipmaker's customers, including companies like Anthropic, the Wall Street Journal reported.

Market Reaction and Risks

Nvidia stock closed down 2.9% at $217.55 on Monday following the announcement. Barron's noted that the deals are unlikely to ease concerns about circular financing in the AI ecosystem, where Nvidia sits at the center of a web of investment between cloud providers, chip makers, and AI labs. The arrangement gives Nvidia upside if funding supports more AI demand, but it also increases the company's exposure in a potential downturn.

"We began by building chips. Today, we are helping create a new class of productive, investable infrastructure: AI factories."

— Jensen Huang, CEO, Nvidia

What's Next

The six financial partners will work to finalize terms and begin deploying capital, though Nvidia has not set a public timeline. The scale of the initiative — $500 billion in third-party capital with Nvidia potentially backstopping a quarter of it — would make these platforms among the largest dedicated financing vehicles in the technology sector. As AI infrastructure spending accelerates toward Goldman Sachs' $1.64 trillion projection for the decade, Nvidia is positioning itself not just as the dominant chip supplier but as a financial intermediary shaping how the buildout gets funded.
author: Diaspora Desk
